results.question: How do Temporal, Celery and AWS Step Functions each detect a worker that dies in the middle of a task, and what does each do to recover?

team.text:
**Short answer:** None of the three has a real "is this worker alive?" probe for a task in flight. Temporal and Step Functions infer a dead worker from timeouts and missed heartbeats, and both can retry the work automatically. Celery detects a dead child process locally, and detects a lost node only through broker acknowledgement and redelivery rules. By default Celery does not re-run a task whose worker died.

## Temporal

**Detection**
- The server does not notice a crash directly. A task can be lost in delivery, or the worker can crash after calling the activity function. The service relies on the Start-To-Close timeout (https://docs.temporal.io/activity-execution).
- Every activity needs a Start-To-Close or Schedule-To-Close timeout, because the service cannot tell when a worker crashes or loses contact (https://docs.temporal.io/evaluate/features/timeouts-and-retries).
- Long-running activities should heartbeat and set a Heartbeat Timeout, which detects a lost worker sooner than a long Start-To-Close (https://docs.temporal.io/evaluate/features/timeouts-and-retries). A heartbeat is a ping from the worker to the service saying the activity is progressing and the worker has not crashed (https://docs.temporal.io/develop/python/failure-detection).
- Schedule-To-Start covers "no workers available or keeping up", not a mid-execution crash. It never triggers a retry (https://docs.temporal.io/evaluate/features/timeouts-and-retries).

**Recovery of activities**
- When Start-To-Close fires, the server records `ActivityTaskTimedOut`, re-adds the task to the task queue under the Retry Policy, and increments the attempt count (https://temporal.io/blog/activity-timeouts).
- Because the task returns to the shared queue, it is retried on a different worker, according to a Temporal developer. Retries continue until Schedule-To-Close, after which an `ActivityFailure` reaches the workflow code. Maximum attempts of 1 disables retries (https://community.temporal.io/t/workflow-and-activity-timeout/4745).
- An activity failure never fails the workflow unless the workflow code does so deliberately (https://docs.temporal.io/develop/python/failure-detection).

**Recovery of workflow code**
- If a worker dies during a workflow task, the Workflow Task Timeout (default 10 s) elapses. The service records `WorkflowTaskTimedOut` and schedules a new task. A new worker fetches the Event History and replays the workflow code to restore state (https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/event-history/event-history-java).
- Sticky queues speed up the normal case. If a worker does not start a task from its sticky queue within 5 s by default, the service reschedules it on the shared queue (https://github.com/temporalio/sdk-rust/blob/main/arch_docs/sticky_queues.md, https://docs.temporal.io/sticky-execution). A longer sticky timeout means slower failover from a dead worker (https://community.temporal.io/t/workflowtasktimedout/6932).

**Not verified:** the default Heartbeat Timeout (probably unset, so heartbeating is optional) and the default retry policy values. The researcher believed these are 1 s initial interval, 2.0 backoff and unlimited attempts, but no source confirmed it.

## Celery

**Detection**
- With the prefork pool, the parent process monitors its children. If a child is killed (for example by an OOM SIGKILL), the parent marks the task failed with `WorkerLostError('Worker exited prematurely: signal 9 (SIGKILL).')` (https://github.com/celery/billiard/issues/380, https://github.com/celery/celery/issues/5690). It then spawns a replacement child. The container keeps running, so Kubernetes reports nothing (https://engineering.backmarket.com/a-story-of-kubernetes-celery-resource-and-a-rabbit-ec2ef9e37e9f).
- `worker_lost_wait` sets how long to wait for a result that may already have been published before raising `WorkerLostError` (https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/userguide/configuration.html).
- For loss of a whole worker or node, detection happens at the broker: unacknowledged messages are redelivered when the connection closes or the visibility timeout is exceeded (https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/v5.5.1/history/whatsnew-3.0.html). I could not retrieve sources on `broker_heartbeat` or RabbitMQ dead-consumer detection, so the connection-closed claim rests only on that 3.0 page.

**Recovery**
- **Default (`acks_late=False`):** the message is acknowledged just before the task runs (https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/main/reference/celery.app.task.html). So the broker has already discarded it, and the task is not re-run. It shows as failed with `WorkerLostError`. This is inferred from that doc and the issue logs, not stated in one sentence.
- **`acks_late=True`:** the message is acknowledged after the task runs, and the docs warn the task may execute twice if the worker crashes mid-execution (same page). Even so, the worker acknowledges the task if the child process abruptly exits or is signaled. To get redelivery in that case, enable `task_reject_on_worker_lost` (https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/userguide/tasks.html). Wolt recommends combining the two settings (https://careers.wolt.com/en/blog/tech/5-tips-for-writing-production-ready-celery-tasks).
- **Caveats:** a user reports that with this setting, `AsyncResult.get()` still raises `WorkerLostError` even though the task is rescheduled (https://github.com/celery/celery/issues/4229). A recent PR describes an edge case where a child dies after the task succeeded, and the task is requeued and runs again (https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/10752).
- **Visibility timeout (Redis):** a task not acknowledged within the timeout is redelivered to another worker. The default is 1 hour (https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/getting-started/backends-and-brokers/redis.html). A task running longer than the timeout can be picked up by a second worker while the first is still running it (https://dev.to/artemooon/celery-redis-at-scale-designing-a-reliable-and-efficient-task-queue-in-production-27nh).

**Not established:** the current default of `task_reject_on_worker_lost` (docs show `None`, read as off). Retries (`autoretry_for`, `task.retry`) were not covered. My inference is that they apply only to exceptions raised inside the task, not to a lost worker.

## AWS Step Functions

**Detection**
- Step Functions has no worker health check. It uses timeouts and heartbeats. A task waits for a success or failure response within `TimeoutSeconds`, and if none arrives the task fails (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-task.html).
- `HeartbeatSeconds` must be a positive integer smaller than `TimeoutSeconds`. If more time than that passes between heartbeats, the state fails with `States.Timeout` (same page). Workers send heartbeats with `SendTaskHeartbeat` using the task token (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSJavaSDK/latest/javadoc/com/amazonaws/services/stepfunctions/AWSStepFunctionsClient.html).
- The default for both timeouts is 99,999,999 seconds. Without an explicit timeout, a task can wait indefinitely for a response that never comes (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/sfn-best-practices.html). For callback (`.waitForTaskToken`) tasks, AWS recommends adding `HeartbeatSeconds` (same page).

**Recovery**
- `Retry` is a list of retriers with `ErrorEquals`, `IntervalSeconds`, `MaxAttempts` and `BackoffRate`. Defaults reported by secondary sources are 1 s, 3 attempts and 2.0 (https://dev.to/dashbird/aws-step-functions-error-handling-49d0, https://dashbird.io/blog/aws-step-functions-error-handling/). I did not retrieve the official AWS page for these.
- Timeouts can be retried, for example a `States.Timeout` retrier with `MaxAttempts: 2` (https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-12-handle-errors-retries-step-functions/view). Retriers are evaluated in order, so specific ones go before `States.ALL`.
- Once retries are exhausted, `Catch` routes to a fallback state, optionally using `ResultPath` to attach the error (same oneuptime source). A timeout catch often leads to a `Fail` state or a compensation step (https://dev.to/aws-builders/mastering-aws-step-functions-error-handling-j39).
- For Activities, a retry plausibly makes a new task available to the next `GetActivityTask` poll, so another worker can take it. This is my inference, not something I found stated.

**Not verified:** `MaxDelaySeconds`, `JitterStrategy`, and billing treatment of retries.

## Comparison

| | Temporal | Celery | Step Functions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Detection | Timeouts, plus optional activity heartbeats. The service cannot see a crash directly. | Parent notices a dead child immediately. Node loss is detected via the broker connection and visibility timeout. | `TimeoutSeconds` and optional `HeartbeatSeconds` |
| Default if no timeout is set | Start-To-Close or Schedule-To-Close is required | Not applicable. Redis visibility timeout is 1 h. | 99,999,999 s, so effectively waits forever |
| Automatic re-run by default | Yes, under the Retry Policy | No. The task fails with `WorkerLostError` unless `acks_late` and `reject_on_worker_lost` are set. | No. Retry or Catch must be configured. |
| Workflow or orchestration state | Rebuilt by replay on another worker | None. Celery has no central tracker of tasks in flight (my inference). | The state machine is managed by the service |

**Guarantees and idempotency:** all three give at-least-once behaviour once recovery is on, so tasks should be idempotent.
- **Temporal:** a timed-out activity may already have partly run before it is retried.
- **Celery:** the docs explicitly warn of double execution with `acks_late`. Duplicates can also come from the visibility timeout or the post-success edge case.
- **Step Functions:** a timed-out worker may still be running when a retry hands the work to another one. This follows from the timeout design rather than a source I retrieved.

single.text:
**Short answer:** Temporal and Step Functions detect a dead worker with timeouts and heartbeats that the service enforces. Celery has no heartbeat that tracks a running task. It relies on the broker, so recovery depends on settings, and by default a task killed mid-run is lost. The project passages you supplied cover only the project's own supervisor, not these three systems. Everything below comes from web sources.

**Temporal**
- **Detection:** Temporal's docs say the Server doesn't detect failures when a Worker loses communication with the Server or crashes, so it relies on the Start-To-Close Timeout to force Activity failures. The Start-To-Close timeout is one of the timeouts Temporal uses to detect whether an individual Worker has crashed. [https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/detecting-activity-failures]
- **Faster detection with heartbeats:** An Activity can also heartbeat. If the Temporal Service does not receive a Heartbeat within a Heartbeat Timeout, the Activity is considered failed. [https://docs.temporal.io/develop/dotnet/activities/timeouts]
- **Recovery:** After a failure, another Activity Task Execution may be scheduled according to the Retry Policy. A community answer from Temporal says that after a worker crash, the activity can be retried on a different worker process. [https://community.temporal.io/t/workflow-and-activity-timeout/4745] Heartbeat details can carry progress. If an Activity gets retried, it can access the details from the last heartbeat. [https://zio-temporal.vhonta.dev/docs/resilience/heartbeats]

**Celery**
- **Detection:** I found no heartbeat-based detection of a dead task. The broker only notices that the message was never acknowledged. For Redis, if a task isn't acknowledged within the visibility timeout, it will be redelivered to another worker and executed. [Celery Redis broker docs: https://github.com/celery/celery/blob/f6198f59572444efff4ff273de03607e70297faf/docs/getting-started/brokers/redis.rst] Separately, when a pool process is killed, the worker raises `WorkerLostError`. [https://celery-safwan.readthedocs.io/en/latest/userguide/configuration.html] That page is a third-party mirror of the Celery docs, not the official site.
- **Recovery depends on configuration:**
  - By default, Celery drops the task from the broker as soon as the worker acknowledges it (task_acks_late=False), so it can be lost if the worker shuts down before finishing.
  - With `task_acks_late=True`, the broker will redeliver the task if the worker shuts down during execution. [https://www.vintasoftware.com/blog/guide-django-celery-tasks]
  - Even with late acks, the worker acknowledges the task when the worker process executing it abruptly exits or is signaled (e.g. KILL). Setting `task_reject_on_worker_lost` to true lets the message be re-queued instead. [https://celery-safwan.readthedocs.io/en/latest/userguide/configuration.html]
- **Caveats:**
  - With Redis, a long visibility timeout only delays redelivery of 'lost' tasks after a power failure or forced termination. [Celery Redis docs, link above]
  - A task that runs longer than the visibility timeout is executed again on another worker. [Same Redis docs]
  - Redelivery can therefore produce duplicates, so tasks should be idempotent. That is my inference, not a quote from the docs.
  - Some GitHub issues report acked-and-lost tasks in edge cases, such as cold shutdown (celery/billiard#463). I did not verify them.

**AWS Step Functions**
- **Detection:** You set `TimeoutSeconds` and `HeartbeatSeconds` on a Task state. In AWS's example, a task that fails to complete within 300 seconds, or doesn't send heartbeats every 60 seconds, is marked as failed. [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/state-task.html] Workers send heartbeats with `SendTaskHeartbeat`, which resets the Heartbeat clock. [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/stepfunctions/send-task-heartbeat.html] Heartbeats apply to activity workers and callback (task-token) tasks. [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/boto3/latest/reference/services/stepfunctions/client/send_task_heartbeat.html]
- **Error raised:** `States.HeartbeatTimeout` means a Task state failed to send a heartbeat for longer than HeartbeatSeconds. It is available inside the Catch and Retry fields. [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/en_us/step-functions/latest/dg/concepts-error-handling.html] A task that runs past `TimeoutSeconds` raises `States.Timeout`.
- **Recovery:** The state machine's `Retry` rules re-run the task after a backoff, and `Catch` routes to a fallback state. The Dashbird blog gives an example with two retries after waits of 3 and 4.5 seconds. [https://dashbird.io/blog/aws-step-functions-error-handling/] That is a third-party source. I did not pull the official Retry page.

**Comparison**

| | Detector | Recovery |
|---|---|---|
| Temporal | Start-To-Close timeout, optional Heartbeat Timeout | Retry Policy, new attempt on any worker |
| Celery | Unacked message (visibility timeout) or `WorkerLostError` | Redelivery only with `acks_late` plus `reject_on_worker_lost` (or visibility timeout) |
| Step Functions | `TimeoutSeconds`, `HeartbeatSeconds` | `Retry` and `Catch` in the state machine |

I didn't find an official Celery page on this, so the Celery details rest on mirrors and blogs. Check them against the Celery docs for your version.

verdict.reason: A is more thorough and accurate on the key mechanics: Temporal workflow-task recovery via replay and sticky queues, Celery's prefork parent noticing a dead child and the acks_late / reject_on_worker_lost interplay, and Step Functions' 99,999,999 s default and States.Timeout retries. It also flags what it could not verify. B is correct but thinner, leans on a third-party Celery mirror, and omits workflow-level recovery. B has one oddity: a stray reference to "project passages you supplied".'

results.question: What delivery guarantees do Redis Pub/Sub, Redis Streams with consumer groups, and Apache Kafka consumer groups each give a consumer that restarts, and which is the lightest option that does not lose messages?

team.text:
**Short answer:** Redis Streams with consumer groups is the lightest option of the three that does not lose messages across a consumer restart, provided persistence is configured. Pub/Sub loses messages. Kafka also avoids loss, but it is heavier. The Streams and Kafka claims below are mostly not verified against official documentation, so check them before relying on them.

**Redis Pub/Sub: at-most-once, loses messages across a restart (sourced)**
- The official docs describe delivery as "once if at all". If the subscriber hits an error or a network disconnect, the message is "forever lost" (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/pubsub/).
- Messages go only to clients subscribed at publish time. A subscriber that is offline when a message is published misses it, and Redis's guide advises keeping durable state in keys or a Stream (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/pub-sub/dotnet/).
- It follows that a restarting consumer misses everything published while it was down. The official page does not literally say "no replay". That is an inference from the wording above.
- The Redis docs point to Streams for stronger guarantees. They say stream messages are persisted and support at-most-once and at-least-once delivery (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/pubsub/).

**Redis Streams with consumer groups: at-least-once, with caveats (mostly unverified)**
- Confirmed: a stream is an append-only log. Producers append with XADD, and consumers in a group read with XREADGROUP (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/streaming/redis-py/).
- The details below come from background knowledge and were not checked against the official pages:
  - Delivered but unacknowledged entries stay in the group's pending entries list (PEL), tied to a consumer name.
  - Reading with `>` returns only never-delivered entries. Reading with `0` returns the consumer's own pending entries, so a restarted consumer can re-process them.
  - XACK removes an entry from the PEL.
  - XCLAIM and XAUTOCLAIM let another consumer take over entries that have sat idle too long.
  - Together these give at-least-once delivery, so duplicates are possible.
- Durability depends on configuration, also unverified:
  - RDB snapshots can lose recent writes.
  - AOF with `appendfsync everysec` can lose about a second of writes. `always` is safest but slowest.
  - Replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose acknowledged writes. WAIT reduces that risk but does not eliminate it.
- Pages to check: https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/streams/, https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/persistence/, https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/replication/

**Kafka consumer groups: at-least-once if you commit after processing (not verified from Kafka's docs)**
- The only sourced point is from a client library's docs, not Kafka's own. The default auto-commit can lose data on a critical failure, so set `enable_auto_commit=False` and commit manually after processing (https://aiokafka.readthedocs.io/en/stable/examples/manual_commit.html).
- Background knowledge, unverified:
  - Offsets are stored in the internal `__consumer_offsets` topic, and a restarted consumer resumes from its committed offset.
  - Committing after processing gives at-least-once delivery. Committing before gives at-most-once.
  - Exactly-once needs transactions and `read_committed`, and applies to Kafka-to-Kafka flows.
  - Retention limits on offsets and logs matter, and `auto.offset.reset` governs what happens when no committed offset exists.
- I could not retrieve the official Kafka pages ("Message Delivery Semantics", the consumer configs, and the KRaft operations section).

**Which is lightest without losing messages**
- If you already run Redis, use Streams with consumer groups. It needs no new infrastructure, and a restarted consumer can recover its pending entries.
- For the guarantee to hold, enable AOF persistence (`everysec` or `always`) and acknowledge only after processing succeeds.
- Make processing idempotent, for example by deduplicating on the stream entry ID. Redelivery after a crash between processing and XACK is expected under at-least-once.
- Kafka becomes justified when you need very high throughput, long-term retention and replay, many independent consumer groups, or replicated durability without Redis's asynchronous-replication gap. That comparison is my own judgment, since the operational weight of Kafka was not sourced. Kafka also means running brokers and managing partitions.

single.text:
**Short answer:** Redis Streams with consumer groups is the lightest option that doesn't lose messages, provided Redis is already in your stack. Your project already uses it that way. Pub/Sub can lose messages across a restart. Kafka gives a similar guarantee but needs a whole extra system.

**Redis Pub/Sub: at-most-once, so a restart loses messages**
- Redis documents it as at-most-once. A message is delivered once if at all, and Redis never resends it. [https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/pubsub/]
- If your subscriber wasn't attached at publish time, the message is gone. [https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/pub-sub/dotnet/]
- A subscriber that is offline when a message is published misses it permanently. Redis suggests pairing Pub/Sub with durable state if you need replay. [https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/pub-sub/nodejs/]

**Redis Streams with consumer groups: at-least-once, and the consumer resumes after a restart**
- Entries that have been delivered to a consumer but not yet acknowledged stay in a pending entries list. [https://redis.io/blog/simplifying-streams-and-strings/]
- The consumer calls `XACK` after processing, which lets Redis drop the entry from that list. [https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/streaming/java-jedis/]
- After a restart, the consumer re-reads its pending entries by passing an explicit ID instead of `>`. `>` means "entries not yet delivered to anyone". [https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/streaming/java-jedis/]
- A third-party guide (not Redis's own docs) describes this as at-least-once delivery even if a consumer crashes. [https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-31-redis-xreadgroup-consumer-groups/view]
- The catch is that an entry processed but not yet acknowledged when the consumer crashes will be delivered again. Handlers need to tolerate duplicates.

**Kafka consumer groups: at-least-once if you commit after processing**
- A consumer that takes over resumes from the last committed offset. It may repeat the last batch, which is what Kafka calls "at-least-once". [https://kafka.apache.org/10/javadoc/org/apache/kafka/clients/consumer/KafkaConsumer.html]
- Automatic offset commits can also give at-least-once. This only holds if you fully process everything each `poll` returns before the next `poll` or before closing. [https://kafka.apache.org/22/javadoc/org/apache/kafka/clients/consumer/KafkaConsumer.html]
- Committing offsets before processing would lose messages on a crash. Commit after processing. [https://www.conduktor.io/glossary/kafka-consumer-groups-explained]
- Exactly-once needs idempotent producers and transactional APIs (same Conduktor page). That is more than the other two options need.

**Which is lightest?** Redis Streams with consumer groups. It gives the same at-least-once guarantee as Kafka without a broker cluster. Your project already runs Redis, so it adds no new infrastructure.

**How this matches your project docs**
- ROADMAP.md says Redis Streams was chosen because Pub/Sub drops messages when the consumer is slow or restarting.
- README.md says the supervisor reads the event stream through a consumer group, so it resumes after a restart.
- The scorecard in README.md reports "Supervisor restart mid-run" at 8/8 correct. That is a measured result from the fault-injection harness. It covers the supervisor's restart, not a general proof of no loss.
- The last scorecard row says finished subgoals re-run after a crash is "not measured, recovery not built". So the at-least-once duplicate-delivery caveat above hasn't been checked in your system.

**What I didn't verify**
- I didn't find Redis's own page on pending-entry reclaim after a consumer dies permanently (`XAUTOCLAIM`/`XCLAIM`). If a consumer never comes back under the same name, you need that.
- The at-least-once label for Streams comes from a third-party page. Redis's docs describe the pending-list and `XACK` mechanism but, in what I retrieved, didn't use that label.

verdict.reason: B ties nearly every Redis Streams and Kafka claim to a checkable source, including Kafka's own javadoc, and marks the one gap (the third-party at-least-once label). A leaves most Streams and Kafka claims unsourced and cites only a client library for Kafka. B also references project docs the asker presumably has, though that is extra; the sourcing and verified Kafka semantics are what decide it.

results.question: What span names and attributes do the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions define for agent invocations, model calls and tool calls, and what is their current stability status?

team.text:
**Short answer:** The OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions define span names and attributes for agent invocations, model calls and tool calls, but all of it is still **Development** (not Stable). The only Stable attributes are generic ones reused from elsewhere, such as `error.type` and `server.port`. Several details below could not be checked against the full primary pages and are flagged.

## Where the spec lives
- The opentelemetry.io semconv index (v1.44.0) says the GenAI conventions have "Moved to the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions repository." https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/
- The main repo's release notes list a breaking change: the GenAI conventions moved to a dedicated repository (#3696). https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/releases
- The new home is `open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai`, under `docs/gen-ai/`: https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-agent-spans.md
- The v1.41.0 snapshot of the old repo is still readable: https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/blob/v1.41.0/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-spans.md
- Secondary sources say the old opentelemetry.io `gen-ai` pages are now redirect stubs (https://www.dash0.com/knowledge/opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions-explained).
- One article dates the move to June 2026 (https://www.truefoundry.com/blog/opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions). This is unverified.

## 1. Agent invocations
The agent-spans document has these sections: Create agent, Invoke agent client, Invoke agent internal, Invoke workflow, Plan, Execute tool, and agent-skill spans (Load skill, Read skill resource, Command execution). https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/blob/main/docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-agent-spans.md

**Invoke agent (client span)**
- It describes invocation of a remote agent service and is marked Status: Development.
- `gen_ai.operation.name` SHOULD be `invoke_agent`.
- The span name SHOULD be `invoke_agent {gen_ai.agent.name}` if the name is readily available, otherwise `invoke_agent`. Frameworks MAY use another format.
- Span kind SHOULD be CLIENT.
- Older text allowed INTERNAL for in-process agents (https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/issues/308). The newer split into client and internal sections appears to replace it.

**Create agent**
- Name: `create_agent {gen_ai.agent.name}`. `gen_ai.operation.name` is `create_agent`. Kind SHOULD be CLIENT.
- `gen_ai.operation.name` and `gen_ai.provider.name` are Required.
- `error.type` is Conditionally Required on error. It is the only Stable attribute here.
- `gen_ai.agent.id`, `gen_ai.agent.name`, `gen_ai.agent.description` and `gen_ai.agent.version` are Conditionally Required. `gen_ai.agent.id` should be the provider-assigned stable identifier for hosted agents, and recording in-memory instance ids on it is NOT RECOMMENDED.
- This table came from a registry search snippet, not a full page read.

**Not established:** I did not retrieve the span names or attribute tables for the Invoke agent internal, Invoke workflow (`invoke_workflow`) and Plan (`plan`) spans. A secondary source suggests `gen_ai.agent.id`, `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id` (https://www.morphllm.com/agent-tracing). Check the primary file for requirement levels.

Release notes for v1.38.0 mention a `gen_ai.tool.definitions` attribute on the `invoke_agent` span (https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions/releases/tag/v1.38.0).

## 2. Model calls (inference)
- Span name SHOULD be `{gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.request.model}`, e.g. `chat gpt-4`. Systems MAY use a different format. (v1.41.0 gen-ai-spans.md, URL above)
- Span kind SHOULD be CLIENT. It MAY be INTERNAL for models running in-process. Status follows the Recording Errors document.
- `gen_ai.operation.name` well-known values for model calls are `chat`, `text_completion`, `generate_content` and `embeddings`. If one applies it MUST be used. Other values in the registry include `create_agent`, `execute_tool`, `invoke_agent`, `invoke_workflow`, `retrieval`, `plan` and the memory operations. All are Development. https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/registry/attributes/gen-ai/
- Confirmed attributes:
  - `gen_ai.operation.name` and `gen_ai.provider.name` are Required.
  - `gen_ai.request.model` is Conditionally Required if available.
  - `error.type` is Conditionally Required on error.
  - `server.address` and `server.port` are listed.
  - `gen_ai.system_instructions` is Opt-In.

## 3. Tool calls (`execute_tool`)
From v1.41.0 (Development):

  - `gen_ai.tool.call.arguments` and `gen_ai.tool.call.result` are Opt-In.

A variant adds `{gen_ai.skill.resource.name}`. The newer text also says kind SHOULD be INTERNAL, but it is unclear whether that applies to this span alone or to the whole section.

## Stability and opt-in guidance
- **Status:** the spans documents and attribute values read are all marked Development. Secondary sources agree that GenAI and MCP conventions remained in Development as of May 2026 (https://hidekazu-konishi.com/entry/opentelemetry_genai_semantic_conventions_guide.html, https://greptime.com/blogs/2026-05-09-opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions, https://dev.to/azena-ai/opentelemetrys-genai-semantic-conventions-are-not-stable-yet-heres-what-actually-shipped-in-2026-3mke).

Without it, instrumentation written before v1.37 keeps emitting the older format by default. Sources: https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/instrumentation/otel_instrumentation/ and the Greptime blog above. I did not find the official text on other values for this variable, such as a dual-emit option.
- **Caveats:**
  - Attribute names have changed between releases. Per secondary sources:
    - v1.37 replaced `gen_ai.system` with `gen_ai.provider.name`.
    - `gen_ai.usage.prompt_tokens` became `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`.
    - `gen_ai.prompt` and `gen_ai.completion` were deprecated and removed as of v1.38.0 (https://github.com/traceloop/openllmetry/issues/3515).

results.question: How do LangGraph, CrewAI and the OpenAI Agents SDK each handle a failed or stuck step in a multi-agent run, in terms of retries, timeouts and checkpoints?

team.text:
**Short answer:** I can't give a verified three-way comparison. The research behind this answer was cut short by search-tool limits, and only a handful of facts were confirmed. Below is what is sourced, followed by what is still unknown. I have not filled the gaps from memory.

## What is confirmed

| | Retries | Timeouts | Checkpoints / resume |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LangGraph** | `RetryPolicy` applies per node attempt, with exponential backoff, optional jitter, and a configurable predicate for which exceptions are retryable. The example showed `initial_interval=0.5` and `backoff_factor=2.0`. ([LangChain blog](https://www.langchain.com/blog/fault-tolerance-in-langgraph)) | Not confirmed. The blog title mentions timeouts, but that part was not read. | Not confirmed. |
| **CrewAI** | The Agents page summary describes `max_retry_limit` as retries on error. Its default was not seen. `max_iter` caps iterations before the agent must give its best answer (default 20). `max_rpm` limits requests per minute to avoid rate limits. ([CrewAI Agents docs](https://docs.crewai.com/v1.15.23/en/concepts/agents)) | `max_execution_time` is described as a timeout in seconds. Whether it stops a stuck step or only limits total time was not confirmed. ([same page](https://docs.crewai.com/v1.15.23/en/concepts/agents)) | Not confirmed. |
| **OpenAI Agents SDK** | Not confirmed. | Not confirmed. | Not confirmed. |

The OpenAI Agents SDK's `Runner.run` raises `MaxTurnsExceeded` when `max_turns` is exceeded "unless handled", and raises the matching tripwire exception, such as `InputGuardrailTripwireTriggered`, when a guardrail trips. This is a loop cap and a guardrail stop, not a retry or timeout. Only the opening snippet of the page was seen, so how the "unless handled" mechanism works is unconfirmed. ([Runner.run reference](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/ref/run/))

## Gaps: not verified, so no claims are made

- **LangGraph:** the full `RetryPolicy` parameters and defaults, node timeouts, `recursion_limit`, checkpointers and resuming from the last checkpoint, and time travel and durable execution modes.
- **CrewAI:** task guardrails and their retry behavior, Flow error handling, Flow state persistence, crew replay from a task, and any other checkpointing.
- **OpenAI Agents SDK:** model and API retry settings, per-call or per-tool timeouts, tool-failure handling, session persistence, run-state serialization and resumption, durable-execution integrations, and whether any built-in checkpointing exists.

Because these were not found, I can't say whether any of the three frameworks lacks built-in support for a given feature. "Not confirmed" above means unchecked, not absent.

## Where to check next

- **LangGraph:** the persistence, durable execution, time travel and recursion-limit pages at docs.langchain.com, plus the [`RetryPolicy` API reference](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langgraph/types/RetryPolicy).
- **CrewAI:** the tasks, flows and CLI pages at docs.crewai.com.
- **OpenAI Agents SDK:** the running agents, sessions, guardrails, tools and human-in-the-loop pages at openai.github.io/openai-agents-python, plus the exceptions reference.

**Short answer:** all three have retries and timeouts, but they work at different levels. Only LangGraph gives a clear, documented checkpoint-based recovery. I could not confirm CrewAI's or the OpenAI Agents SDK's checkpoint and resume behaviour, because my search limit ran out. None of the project passages you supplied (Concord's README, tracing and roadmap) describe these three frameworks, so everything below comes from the frameworks' own docs.

**LangGraph**
- **Retries:** these are set per node. `add_node(..., retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=5))` is the form shown, and `retry_on` can limit retries to specific exceptions. [https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/use-graph-api]
- **Timeouts:** these are also per node, and they apply to each attempt. Node timeouts work only for async nodes, and a sync node with a timeout raises an error at compile time. An overrun raises `NodeTimeoutError`. If the retry policy covers it, the timed-out attempt is retried. [same URL]
- **Checkpoints:** checkpointers save a thread's graph state as checkpoints, and the docs list fault tolerance among their uses. [https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence] The docs' own advice is to combine a retry policy with `timeout=` to cap each attempt and to see the "Fault tolerance" page for the full lifecycle. [https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/thinking-in-langgraph] I did not read that page, so I can't say exactly what is restored after a crash.

**CrewAI**
- **Retries:** agent settings include `max_iter`, which is the maximum iterations before the agent must provide its best answer, and `max_rpm` for rate limits. [https://docs.crewai.com/v1.15.23/en/concepts/agents] A third-party wrapper documents `max_retry_limit` as retries per agent after recoverable failures. [http://genai.datarobot.com/api/crewai/agent/] That is not CrewAI's own page, so check it against the official docs. Tasks with a guardrail can be retried too, capped by `guardrail_max_retries`. [https://docs.crewai.com/en/concepts/tasks]
- **Timeouts:** `max_execution_time` is the maximum time in seconds for task execution. [https://docs.crewai.com/v1.15.23/en/concepts/agents]
- **Checkpoints:** I did not find this in the sources I retrieved, so I can't state it either way.

**OpenAI Agents SDK**
- **Retries:** `ModelSettings.retry` holds opt-in, runner-managed retry settings for model calls. [https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/ref/model_settings/] The JS SDK docs add that retries happen only when the policy opts in and the request is safe to replay, or the app approves an unsafe replay. [https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/models/]
- **Timeouts:** `ModelSettings.timeout` is the maximum duration in seconds for each model-call attempt. It does not bound the full run, tool calls, or retry backoff. [same ref page] The run-level limit is a turn count: exceeding `max_turns` raises `MaxTurnsExceeded`, and `max_turns=None` disables the limit. [https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/running_agents/] A `RunErrorHandlerResult` hook appears in that page's example for handling this, but I only saw a snippet of it.
- **Checkpoints:** I did not confirm any built-in checkpoint or resume mechanism. The running-agents page mentions session defaults, but I did not read what they do on failure.

**Gaps:** I did not verify CrewAI's checkpoint or resume feature, the OpenAI Agents SDK's checkpoint or resume feature, or the exact contents of LangGraph's restore-after-failure behaviour. Read the pages named above before relying on any of these.

verdict.reason: B gives sourced, specific coverage of retries and timeouts for all three frameworks (LangGraph per-node RetryPolicy and NodeTimeoutError, CrewAI max_execution_time and guardrail retries, OpenAI ModelSettings.retry and timeout). It flags its gaps honestly, including the checkpoint behaviour it could not confirm. A leaves most cells as 'not confirmed' and gives much less usable content, including nothing on OpenAI retries or timeouts.

results.question: According to the MAST taxonomy from the paper 'Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?', what are the three failure categories, and which individual failure modes are most common?

team.text:
**The three MAST failure categories** (Cemri et al., "Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?", arXiv 2503.13657; https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657). MAST has 14 failure modes grouped into three categories:

1. **System design issues** (FC1, also called "specification issues" in later papers)
2. **Inter-agent misalignment** (FC2)
3. **Task verification** (FC3)

**Most common individual failure modes.** The per-mode figures below come from Figure 1 of arXiv v3 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.13657), which reports prevalence across 1,642 traces. Most of the mode-to-number mapping was reconstructed from scrambled PDF text, so treat the individual values as likely but not directly confirmed.
1. Step Repetition (1.3): 15.7%
2. Reasoning-Action Mismatch (2.6): 13.2%. A dev.to field guide independently gives the same figure (https://dev.to/tuomo_pisama/a-field-guide-to-multi-agent-failure-modes-59on).
3. Unaware of Termination Conditions (1.5): 12.4%
4. Disobey Task Specification (1.1): 11.8%
5. Incorrect Verification (3.3): 9.1% (inferred)
6. No or Incomplete Verification (3.2): 8.2% (inferred). A secondary blog gives the same 9.1% and 8.2% for these two modes (https://futureagi.substack.com/p/why-do-multi-agent-llm-systems-fail).

Other modes are much rarer. Task Derailment (2.3) is 7.40% and Information Withholding (2.4) is 0.80%, both explicitly confirmed. Conversation Reset (2.1) is 2.20% and Fail to Ask for Clarification (2.2) is 6.80%, also confirmed in the extracted text. I found no prose in the paper that explicitly ranks the modes. The ranking is derived from the figure values.

**Modes by category**
- FC1: Disobey Task Specification (1.1), Disobey Role Specification (1.2), Step Repetition (1.3), Loss of Conversation History (1.4), Unaware of Termination Conditions (1.5). Modes 1.2 and 1.5 were not seen in the NeurIPS text and were filled in from memory. A separate paper (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.17915) lists all five, which supports this.
- FC2: Conversation Reset, Fail to Ask for Clarification, Task Derailment, Information Withholding, Ignored Other Agent's Input, Reasoning-Action Mismatch (2.1–2.6).
- FC3: Premature Termination, No or Incomplete Verification, Incorrect Verification (3.1–3.3).

**Discrepancies between sources**
- **Category shares differ by version.** arXiv v3 Figure 1 gives system design 44.2%, inter-agent misalignment 32.3% and task verification 23.5%. The NeurIPS version gives 41.8%, 36.9% and 21.3% on MAST-Data (210 traces) (https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/b1041e52d3be19f0a9bc491657488e4a-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.pdf). A later paper (arXiv 2606.08162) reports the NeurIPS-style 41.77%, 36.94% and 21.30%. In both versions system design is the largest category and task verification the smallest.
- **Earlier versions had different numbers.** The arXiv PDF text also contains values such as 37.17% for Step Repetition and 7.59% for Reasoning-Action Mismatch. I couldn't tell which version they come from, so cite v3 or the NeurIPS version.
- **Trace counts vary.** The abstract says the taxonomy was developed from 150 traces (inter-annotator kappa = 0.88). The NeurIPS figure uses 210 traces, and arXiv v3 and secondary sources cite about 1,600 or more. These probably refer to different stages of the work, but I did not confirm that.

The first version of the paper called them specification and system design failures, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification and termination [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/389947144_Why_Do_Multi-Agent_LLM_Systems_Fail].
